verified.note: Title, year (2025), journal (JAMA) all match. Abstract confirms exactly: 'screening for IPV in women of reproductive age...and providing or referring those who screen positive to multicomponent interventions has a moderate net benefit...(B recommendation)' and 'benefits and harms of screening for caregiver abuse and neglect in older or vulnerable adults are uncertain...(I statement).' relevance_to_tphe is reasonable and not overstated.

Confirmed by abstract: 'moderate net benefit...The evidence does not support the effectiveness of brief interventions or the provision of information about referral options in the absence of ongoing supportive intervention components. The evidence demonstrating benefit of ongoing support services is predominantly found in studies of pregnant or postpartum women.' Matches key_finding closely.

first_author is wrong: search record lists 'US Preventive Services Task Force' but PubMed indexes the first author as Moyer VA (writing on behalf of USPSTF; this is the standard citation form for this record, e.g. 'Moyer VA; U.S. Preventive Services Task Force'). Content of key_finding is fully supported by the abstract ('The USPSTF recommends that clinicians screen women of childbearing age for IPV...B recommendation...current evidence is insufficient to assess...all elderly or vulnerable adults...I statement'). FIX: change first_author to 'Moyer VA' (or 'Moyer VA, on behalf of the USPSTF').

Title, year (2004), journal (Annals of Internal Medicine), first_author all match. BUT the PubMed abstract for this record is purely procedural/administrative -- it describes the process ('In 1996, the USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against...a grade C recommendation, according to 1996 grade definitions. The USPSTF now uses an explicit process...') and does NOT itself state the 2004 recommendation's actual grade or conclusion text (no 'I statement' or 'insufficient evidence' language about the 2004 finding appears in the abstract retrieved via efetch). The key_finding's specific claim ('USPSTF found the evidence insufficient (I statement) to recommend for or against routine screening instruments...') is historically well-established (corroborated indirectly by PMID 23338828's abstract, which refers to updating '2004' with a new B-grade) but is not directly supported by this record's own PubMed abstract text. FIX: either cite a source that states the 2004 grade explicitly, or soften key_finding to note the grade is inferred from the update history in PMID 23338828 rather than quoted from this abstract.

All specific numbers confirmed verbatim: 'Fifteen fair- and good-quality studies evaluated 13 screening instruments, and six instruments were highly accurate'; 'Fourteen studies indicated minimal adverse effects with screening, but some women experienced discomfort, loss of privacy, emotional distress, and concerns about further abuse'; 'Four fair- and good-quality trials of counseling reported reduced IPV and improved birth outcomes for pregnant women, reduced IPV for new mothers, and reduced pregnancy coercion and unsafe relationships for women in family-planning clinics'; 'A large fair-quality trial of screening versus usual care indicated reduced IPV and improved health outcomes for both groups, but no statistically significant differences between groups.' First author Nelson HD matches.

Numbers checked strictly and confirmed exactly. Identification: 'screening increased clinical identification of victims/survivors (OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.79 to 4.87, moderate quality evidence)' with n=10,074 in the underlying 8 studies -- matches key_finding's 'OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.79-4.87, n=10,074' precisely. Referrals: 'Only two studies (n = 1298) measured referrals to domestic violence support services...We detected no evidence of an effect on referrals (OR 2.24, 95% CI 0.64 to 7.86, low quality evidence)' -- matches key_finding's 'OR 2.24, 95% CI 0.64-7.86, only 2 studies, n=1298' exactly. Re-exposure: 'Only two studies measured women's experience of violence (three to 18 months after screening) and found no evidence that screening decreased IPV' matches '3-18 months' claim. Authors' Conclusions state 'there is insufficient evidence to justify screening in healthcare settings,' supporting the key_finding's summary. 13 trials/n=14,959 also confirmed.

All figures confirmed exactly against full abstract: depression SMD -0.24 (95% CI -0.47 to -0.01; 4 trials, 600 women, moderate-certainty) at medium-term; anxiety 'may reduce anxiety symptoms'; self-efficacy/PTSD/re-exposure/safety-planning all reported as 'no evidence of a difference' / uncertain, matching key_finding's 'uncertain or absent'; and 'only one trial measured harm outcomes using a validated scale' out of 33 trials matches 'only 1 of 33 trials used a validated harm-outcome scale' exactly.

first_author is wrong: search lists 'Kondro W' but PubMed indexes the first author as Eggertson. More importantly, this CMAJ news item has NO abstract in the PubMed record (efetch returns an empty AbstractText for this PMID) -- so the key_finding's specific claims ('call for a first-line, non-judgmental, safety-focused clinical response...the basis of what became the LIVES model') cannot be confirmed against abstract text; they are plausible given the title and corroborated indirectly by other verified records in this set (PMID 25467583, 41267027, 41151831 all reference the WHO 2013 guideline/LIVES model), but this specific record offers no abstract to quote. The search record itself already flags this as 'secondary reporting...useful only as a contemporaneous pointer, not as primary evidence,' which is appropriate hedging. FIX: correct first_author to Eggertson; note in the record that no abstract exists for this PMID so the key_finding is unverifiable from PubMed metadata alone (title-only support).

WHO 2013 clinical/policy guideline ('Responding to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women'), ISBN 978 92 4 154859 5. Not PubMed-indexed as a journal article (confirmed: an esearch for its title returns no exact match, only tangentially related IPV articles -- consistent with it being a WHO monograph rather than a journal record, as the search record itself notes). Not independently fetched or full-text-verified in this pass. in_scope=true because it is corroborated as a genuine, well-known WHO official publication by internal cross-reference: multiple independently-verified PubMed records in this same set explicitly cite the '2013 guidelines published by WHO' (PMID 25467583) and the WHO 'LIVES' model this guideline originates (PMID 41267027, 41151831, 41330529). This corroboration is indirect, not a direct fetch of the WHO document itself -- flag this as a lower-confidence verification tier than the PubMed-fetched records above.

WHO 2014 clinical handbook ('Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook'), WHO/RHR/14.26. Not PubMed-indexed as a journal article (esearch for its title returns no exact match, only broadly related IPV/health-care records). Not independently fetched or full-text-verified in this pass. in_scope=true on the same indirect corroboration basis as the 2013 guideline above -- the LIVES protocol this handbook operationalizes is independently confirmed to exist and be WHO-attributed via PMID 25467583, 41267027, 41151831, 41330529. Same lower-confidence caveat applies: this is corroboration by citation network, not a direct document fetch.

overall_note: 19 of 21 records were fetched directly from PubMed via efetch (all 19 PMIDs resolved and matched on title/year/journal). Of those 19, the two most consequential quantitative claims in the set -- the Cochrane O'Doherty 2015 identification OR (2.95, 95% CI 1.79-4.87) and referral OR (2.24, 95% CI 0.64-7.86), and the Hameed 2020 psychological-therapies depression SMD (-0.24, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.01) -- were checked strictly against the full abstract text and confirmed exact. The Nigeria trial (PMID 41151831) beta values (0.54 and 0.51 with their CIs) were also confirmed exact. The dominant, systematic problem in this record set is NOT fabricated findings but a first_author field that is wrong on 12 of 19 PubMed-indexed records (23338828, 41267027, 41151831, 32460786, 41330529, 34838218, 23917943, 25022633, 32869478, 36693203, 24082017, plus a minor diacritic-only variant on 25467583) -- these appear to have been guessed or drawn from a different citation convention rather than read off the actual PubMed record, and should be corrected before publication since author misattribution in a public-facing manuscript is a real citation-accuracy defect even when the underlying content claims are sound. Two records (14996680 and 24082017) make key_finding claims that could not be directly confirmed from the PubMed abstract text itself (one because the abstract is purely procedural, the other because no abstract exists for this news item) -- both should be softened or sourced elsewhere. The two WHO monographs (no PMID) were, per instructions, not fetched directly; their existence and content are corroborated only indirectly via citation network from the other 19 verified records, which is a real but weaker form of verification -- if these documents are cited with specific quoted claims in the manuscript, an independent direct check of the WHO IRIS documents themselves is recommended before publication. No record in this set was found to be fabricated, off-topic, or out of scope; no DROP verdicts were issued.
